extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners and agents (USPTO registrants); practitioners responsible for filing micro-entity certifications
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and professional duties governing (1) eligibility for micro entity fee reductions (37 C.F.R. §1.29; MPEP §509.04), including how to count prior applications, and (2) practitioner certification and diligence obligations when presenting papers to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. §11.18 et seq.), plus disciplinary and criminal consequences for violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Micro Entity Eligibility — Four statutory certification requirements (37 C.F.R. §1.29 / MPEP §509.04)
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a micro entity, patent applicants must certify that: (1) the applicant qualifies as a small entity as defined in §1.27; (2) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has been named as the inventor or a joint inventor on more than four previously filed patent applications; (3) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor, in the calendar year preceding the calendar year in which the applicable fee is being paid, had a gross income exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year; and (4) neither the applicant nor the inventor nor a joint inventor has assigned, granted, or conveyed, nor is under an obligation by contract or law to assign, grant, or convey, a license or other ownership interest in the application concerned to an entity that had a gross income exceeding three times the median household income for that preceding calendar year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See generally 37 C.F.R. §1.29 and MPEP §509.04 (II. Bases for Establishing Micro Entity Status). The certification must reflect these elements; failure to meet any one disqualifies micro entity treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bases for Establishing Micro Entity Status (gross income basis vs institution of higher education)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two separate bases for establishing micro entity status: the 'gross income basis' under 35 U.S.C. §123(a) and the 'institution of higher education basis' under 35 U.S.C. §123(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §509 describes these bases in detail. The 'gross income' basis includes the previously filed applications limit (see separate criteria). Practitioners must determine which statutory basis applies before certifying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application Filing Limit — Which prior applications count toward the 'more than four previously filed applications' limit
rubrics_metrics.description: For purposes of the 'gross income' basis, the application filing limit includes: (i) previously filed U.S. nonprovisional applications (e.g., utility, design, plant, continuation, and divisional applications), (ii) previously filed U.S. reissue applications, and (iii) previously filed U.S. national stage applications under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §509.04(a) ('B. Application Filing Limit'). 'All such applications naming the inventor or a joint inventor are counted toward the application filing limit, whether the applications were filed before, on, or after March 19, 2013.' It does not matter whether the previously filed applications are pending, patented, or abandoned; they are still included when counting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusions from the Application Filing Limit
rubrics_metrics.description: The application filing limit does not include: (i) foreign applications; (ii) international (PCT) applications for which the basic U.S. national stage filing fee was not paid; and (iii) provisional applications. Also, where an applicant/inventor has assigned, or is under an obligation by contract or law to assign, all ownership rights in the application as the result of previous employment, that person is not considered 'named' on the prior filed application for purposes of determining micro entity status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §509.04(a) ('B. Application Filing Limit'). Apply these exclusions when counting prior applications for micro entity eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-counting nuance — maximum number of micro-entity fee payments may vary
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the four-application limit is a limit on previously filed U.S. nonprovisional applications, reissue applications, and national stage applications, the maximum number of applications in which fees can be paid at the micro entity discount rate can vary from 0 to 5 for any given inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP §509.04(a) explains that the practical impact of counting rules can produce different maxima; practitioners should apply the counting rules carefully to each inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of Micro Entity — form, timing, and payment rule
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 123 requires a certification as a condition for an applicant to be considered a micro entity. The certification must be in writing and must be filed prior to or at the time a fee is first paid in the micro entity amount in an application or patent. A fee may be paid in the micro entity amount only if it is submitted with, or subsequent to, the submission of a certification of entitlement to micro entity status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §509.04 and 37 C.F.R. §1.29(f). Ensure written certification is present before or at the time the micro entity fee is first paid; do not pay the reduced fee without the certification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent establishment or payment of micro entity status is fraud on the Office (37 C.F.R. §1.29(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: Any attempt to fraudulently establish status or pay fees as a micro entity shall be considered as a fraud practiced or attempted on the Office. Improperly, and with intent to deceive, establishing status or paying fees as a micro entity shall be considered as a fraud practiced or attempted on the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. §1.29(j) and MPEP §509.04. Intent to deceive in micro-entity certification is an aggravating issue and may lead to disciplinary or other enforcement consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner certification obligations when presenting papers to the USPTO (37 C.F.R. §11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner certifies when presenting any paper to the USPTO that: statements made on the practitioner's own knowledge are true; statements based on information and belief are believed to be true; and, to the best of the party's knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, (i) the paper is not being presented for any improper purpose (e.g., harassment or needless delay/cost), (ii) legal contentions are warranted by existing law or a nonfrivolous argument for change, (iii) allegations and factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after reasonable investigation, and (iv) denials of factual contentions are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. §11.18(b)(1) and (b)(2) (emphasis added). Practitioners must conduct a 'reasonable inquiry under the circumstances' before signing or presenting certifications (including micro-entity certifications). Failure to do so undermines the practitioner's certification and may expose filings to challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of violating practitioner certification requirements — probative value, criminal exposure, and disciplinary action
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of §11.18 may jeopardize the probative value of the filing. Any false or fraudulent statements are subject to criminal penalty under 18 U.S.C. §1001. Any registered practitioner who violates the provisions of this section may also be subject to disciplinary action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 37 C.F.R. §11.18(b)(1), §11.18(d), and the reference to 18 U.S.C. §1001. Practitioners should recognize both administrative (discipline) and criminal risks from false or insufficiently investigated statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence requirement and conduct prejudicial standards (37 C.F.R. §11.103 and §11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry under the circumstances, to pay adequate attention to certifications presented, or to have adequate procedures in place to ensure compliance can violate 37 C.F.R. §11.103 (diligence) and 37 C.F.R. §11.804(d) (conduct prejudicial to the administration of the patent application process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order treated signing/presenting multiple erroneous micro-entity certifications within a short time-span and relying on the client's erroneous representations (without sufficient verification or procedures) as violations of these rules. Practitioners should implement adequate docketing, verification procedures, and reasonable-investigation practices to satisfy diligence and avoid conduct prejudicial findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning and remedial expectations in discipline matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary actions may include public reprimand, electronic publication of the Final Order in OED's FOIA Reading Room, publication in the Official Gazette, and consideration of the record in future disciplinary matters (including as an aggravating factor). Parties may agree to waivers of reconsideration and appeals as part of a settlement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Final Order describes agreed-upon sanction (public reprimand), publication steps, that each party bears its own costs, and that the Office may consider the record in future proceedings. Remedial steps taken by the practitioner (e.g., improved docketing, custom declaration forms, client counseling, mentorship) were considered mitigating factors.
